dx: Erythema nodosum with acute sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome)
case: A 32-year-old woman comes to the rheumatology clinic because of a 2-week history of painful red lumps on both shins, swollen ankles, and fatigue. Her temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows multiple tender, warm, erythematous, poorly demarcated nodules 2 to 4 cm in diameter over the anterior shins and periarticular swelling of both ankles. There is no ulceration. A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium concentration is 10.9 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity is increased. Diagnosis: erythema nodosum with acute sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome).

questions.stem: A deep incisional biopsy specimen of one shin nodule is obtained. In which of the following sites is the inflammatory infiltrate most likely to be centered?
options: Papillary dermis just beneath the epidermis
Basal layer along the dermal-epidermal junction
Fibrous septa between subcutaneous fat lobules
Fat lobules of the subcutis around inflamed arteries
approach: Recognize tender red nodules on the anterior shins that do not ulcerate as erythema nodosum.
Recall that erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis without vasculitis.
Locate the septa: the fibrous bands that divide the subcutaneous fat into lobules.
questions.why: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis, an inflammation of the subcutaneous fat, and it is centered on the fibrous septa between fat lobules. Early lesions show edema and neutrophils in the septa, and older lesions show lymphocytes, histiocytes, and giant cells with septal fibrosis. There is no vasculitis and little fat necrosis, which is why the nodules heal without scarring or ulceration. It is a reactive pattern linked to streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, endemic fungi, inflammatory bowel disease, pregnancy, and drugs.
whyNot: The papillary dermis is the site of many superficial dermatoses, such as the neutrophilic microabscesses of dermatitis herpetiformis. Erythema nodosum sits much deeper, in the subcutis.
Damage along the basal layer is interface dermatitis, seen in lichen planus and lupus. It produces surface scale and pigment change, not deep tender nodules.
Correct.
Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis describes erythema induratum (nodular vasculitis), which favors the calves and can ulcerate and scar.

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of a hilar lymph node shows tightly packed epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells with no central necrosis. Which of the following signals most directly drives the formation of these lesions?
options: Interferon-gamma from Th1 cells
Interleukin-4 from Th2 cells
Interleukin-17 from Th17 cells
Interleukin-10 from regulatory T cells
approach: Identify the lesion: noncaseating granulomas, the hallmark of sarcoidosis.
Recall that granulomas form when CD4+ Th1 cells activate macrophages.
Name the cytokine: interferon-gamma turns macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells.
questions.why: A granuloma is a focus of chronic inflammation made of activated macrophages. Macrophages present antigen and release IL-12, which drives CD4+ T cells toward the Th1 subset. Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages so they become epithelioid cells and fuse into multinucleated giant cells. TNF-alpha helps hold the granuloma together. Sarcoid granulomas lack central necrosis (noncaseating), while tuberculous granulomas usually have central caseous necrosis.
whyNot: Correct.
IL-4 from Th2 cells drives IgE class switching and allergic, eosinophil-rich inflammation, as in asthma and helminth infection. It does not build granulomas.
IL-17 from Th17 cells recruits neutrophils and defends against extracellular bacteria and fungi at mucosal surfaces. It is central to psoriasis.
IL-10 from regulatory T cells suppresses macrophage activation and would dampen granuloma formation.

questions.stem: Her serum parathyroid hormone concentration is 8 pg/mL (10 to 65). Activated macrophages in her granulomas carry out a conversion that is not regulated by parathyroid hormone. Which of the following conversions most likely explains her hypercalcemia?
options: 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol
Cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D
25-hydroxyvitamin D to 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
approach: Trace the normal pathway: UVB in the epidermis, 25-hydroxylation in the liver, 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney.
Note that low PTH with high calcium means the calcium source is independent of PTH.
Recall that granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which makes active calcitriol without PTH control.
questions.why: Vitamin D is made when UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis to cholecalciferol. The liver adds a 25-hydroxyl group, and the kidney adds the 1-alpha-hydroxyl group to make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), the active hormone. Normally PTH controls the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol production falls when calcium is high. Macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express their own 1-alpha-hydroxylase that ignores this feedback, so calcitriol rises, gut calcium absorption rises, and PTH is suppressed.
whyNot: This UVB-driven step happens in the epidermis. It depends on sun exposure and skin pigment and does not explain PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
The liver does this 25-hydroxylation, and it is loosely regulated. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the storage form and has little activity of its own.
24-hydroxylation produces an inactive metabolite. It is the route the kidney uses to turn vitamin D off when calcium is high.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her hypercalcemia persists for a year without treatment. A renal biopsy specimen shows calcium deposits in the basement membranes of otherwise viable tubules and in the interstitium. Which of the following best describes this process?
options: Dystrophic calcification of necrotic tubular cells
Metastatic calcification of normal tissue
Amyloid deposition with apple-green birefringence
Cholesterol deposition within foamy macrophages
approach: Note the setting: calcium is deposited in living, previously normal tissue.
Link it to the serum: she has sustained hypercalcemia.
Name the process: calcification of normal tissue driven by high serum calcium is metastatic calcification.
questions.why: Pathologic calcification comes in two forms. Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or damaged tissue, such as old infarcts, atheromas, and damaged heart valves, while serum calcium stays normal. Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue when serum calcium or phosphate is high. It favors tissues that lose acid and so have an alkaline interior, such as the kidney tubules, lung alveoli, and gastric mucosa. In the kidney this nephrocalcinosis can impair function, which is one reason hypercalcemia from sarcoidosis is treated.
whyNot: Dystrophic calcification needs prior necrosis and occurs with normal serum calcium. Here the tubules are viable and calcium is high.
Correct.
Amyloid is a proteinaceous deposit identified with Congo red and apple-green birefringence under polarized light. It is not calcium.
Cholesterol-laden foam cells form xanthomas and atheromas. They are lipid infiltrates, not mineral deposits.

case: A 20-year-old man who is on his college wrestling team comes to the student health clinic because of a painful boil on his thigh, his third in 4 months. Two teammates have had similar lesions. His temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). Physical examination shows a 2-cm tender, fluctuant, erythematous nodule on the posterior thigh centered on a hair follicle, with a central pustule. Two healed scars are present nearby. Incision and drainage yields thick yellow pus. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus that is catalase positive, coagulase positive, and resistant to oxacillin. Diagnosis: recurrent furunculosis caused by community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

questions.stem: Three months later he develops fever and a 6-cm indurated, painful plaque on the back of his neck with several openings draining pus. Compared with his thigh lesion, which of the following best describes the extent of this new lesion?
options: Several follicles joined by subcutaneous abscesses
Superficial infection of the upper follicle only
One follicle with an abscess in the deep dermis
Diffuse spread through dermis and subcutis without pus
approach: Place each follicular infection on a depth scale: folliculitis, furuncle, carbuncle.
Note the new features: a large plaque, several draining openings, and fever.
Match them to a carbuncle, which links several infected follicles through the subcutis.
questions.why: Follicular infections are graded by depth and extent. Folliculitis is a superficial pustule at the follicle opening. A furuncle (boil), like his thigh lesion, is a deeper abscess around one follicle that extends into the dermis. A carbuncle is a group of furuncles connected by abscesses in the subcutaneous tissue, with several draining openings, often on the thick skin of the nape or back. Carbuncles more often cause fever and bacteremia. Staphylococcus aureus causes most of these lesions.
whyNot: Correct.
Infection limited to the upper follicle is folliculitis, which produces small pustules. Hot tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas aeruginosa is one example.
A single follicle with a deep dermal abscess is a furuncle, which describes his earlier thigh lesion.
Diffuse spreading infection of the dermis and subcutis without a pus collection is cellulitis.

questions.stem: Molecular typing of his isolate is performed. Which of the following results is most likely?
options: Large SCCmec type II without PVL genes
mecA absent with PVL genes present
Plasmid beta-lactamase gene with TSST-1
Small SCCmec type IV with PVL genes
approach: Oxacillin resistance in S. aureus means the mecA gene is present.
Recall that mecA rides on a mobile element, the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec).
Match the setting: a healthy athlete with recurrent abscesses fits the community strain, which carries small SCCmec types and Panton-Valentine leukocidin.
questions.why: All MRSA strains carry mecA on a mobile genetic island called SCCmec. Hospital strains usually carry large SCCmec types (I, II, III) that also hold other resistance genes, and they rarely make Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL). Community strains usually carry the small type IV element, stay susceptible to more non-beta-lactam drugs, and often make PVL, a pore-forming toxin that kills neutrophils and causes necrotic abscesses and furuncles. They spread through skin contact and shared equipment in athletes, military recruits, prisons, and people who inject drugs. The anterior nares are the main reservoir, which is why recurrent cases may be decolonized.
whyNot: Large SCCmec types without PVL describe hospital-acquired MRSA, seen with catheters, surgery, and long stays in health care settings.
Without mecA the isolate would be susceptible to oxacillin. This pattern fits a PVL-producing methicillin-susceptible strain.
Plasmid penicillinase inactivates penicillin but not oxacillin. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome, not recurrent abscesses.
Correct.

questions.stem: He asks why the cephalexin he was first given did not work. Which of the following best explains the resistance of his isolate to both oxacillin and cephalexin?
options: Secreted beta-lactamase that opens the beta-lactam ring
Altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity
Peptidoglycan precursors ending in D-Ala-D-Lac
Membrane efflux pump that exports beta-lactams
approach: Note that oxacillin is built to resist staphylococcal beta-lactamase, so enzyme breakdown cannot explain resistance to it.
Recall the mecA product: PBP2a, a transpeptidase that beta-lactams bind poorly.
Apply it: PBP2a keeps building the cell wall, so nearly all beta-lactams fail.
questions.why: Beta-lactam drugs kill bacteria by binding penicillin-binding proteins, the transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan. The mecA gene of MRSA encodes PBP2a, which has a low affinity for beta-lactams and keeps cross-linking the wall when the native PBPs are blocked. This makes MRSA resistant to penicillinase-resistant penicillins and to most cephalosporins, including cephalexin. S. aureus itself is a gram-positive coccus in clusters that is catalase and coagulase positive, and protein A on its surface binds the Fc portion of IgG.
whyNot: Most S. aureus strains make penicillinase, which explains penicillin resistance. Oxacillin and related drugs were designed to withstand this enzyme.
Correct.
Changing the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac is the mechanism of vancomycin resistance in enterococci (vanA). It does not affect beta-lactams.
Efflux pumps cause resistance to tetracyclines and macrolides. They are not the basis of methicillin resistance.

questions.stem: Because of his recurrent abscesses, an inherited phagocyte defect is considered. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes would most strongly predispose a patient to recurrent abscesses with catalase-positive organisms such as this one?
options: Myeloperoxidase
Superoxide dismutase
NADPH oxidase
Adenosine deaminase
approach: Recall how neutrophils kill: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, which becomes hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase turns it into hypochlorous acid.
Note that catalase-positive bacteria destroy their own hydrogen peroxide.
So a phagocyte that cannot make superoxide has no oxidant to use against them: chronic granulomatous disease from NADPH oxidase deficiency.
questions.why: The respiratory burst begins when NADPH oxidase in the phagosome membrane transfers electrons from NADPH to oxygen, making superoxide. Superoxide dismutase converts it to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride to make bleach (hypochlorous acid). In chronic granulomatous disease NADPH oxidase is missing. Catalase-negative bacteria leak their own hydrogen peroxide into the phagosome, which the cell can still use, but catalase-positive organisms such as S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, and Aspergillus break it down. The result is recurrent abscesses and granulomas. The dihydrorhodamine flow test or nitroblue tetrazolium test screens for it.
whyNot: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is common and usually silent, with occasional Candida infections. Neutrophils still make hydrogen peroxide and kill most bacteria.
Superoxide dismutase detoxifies superoxide. Inherited loss of SOD1 is linked to familial ALS, not to phagocyte killing defects.
Correct.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, with lymphocyte loss and infections of every type from infancy.

dx: Nonbullous impetigo followed by poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
case: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic because of dark, cola-colored urine and puffy eyes for 2 days. Three weeks ago she had itchy sores around her nose and mouth that formed honey-colored crusts. A culture at that time grew beta-hemolytic, catalase-negative, bacitracin-sensitive gram-positive cocci in chains. Her temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg (above the 95th percentile for her age). Physical examination shows periorbital edema and healed facial skin without scars. Urinalysis shows red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and 1+ protein. Serum C3 concentration is 42 mg/dL (90 to 180). Diagnosis: nonbullous impetigo caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, followed by poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: Her 3-month-old brother develops several large, flaccid bullae on the trunk that rupture and leave shiny erosions with thin brown crusts. A swab grows a coagulase-positive organism. Which of the following mechanisms most likely produces his blisters?
options: Autoantibody binding to desmoglein 3
Exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein 1
Streptococcal hyaluronidase digesting dermal matrix
Autoantibody binding to collagen XVII
approach: Recognize flaccid bullae in an infant with a coagulase-positive organism as bullous impetigo from S. aureus.
Recall that staphylococcal exfoliative toxins are proteases that cut desmoglein 1.
Desmoglein 1 holds keratinocytes together in the upper epidermis, so the split is in the granular layer.
questions.why: Impetigo is a superficial infection of the epidermis in young children. The nonbullous form, with honey-colored crusts, is caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes. The bullous form is caused by S. aureus strains that make exfoliative toxins. These serine proteases cleave desmoglein 1, so keratinocytes separate in the stratum granulosum and form fragile, flaccid bullae. When the toxin spreads through the blood, the same mechanism produces staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Pemphigus foliaceus targets the same protein with autoantibodies.
whyNot: Autoantibodies to desmoglein 3 cause pemphigus vulgaris, an adult disease with a suprabasal split and mouth erosions.
Correct.
Hyaluronidase helps S. pyogenes spread through the dermis in cellulitis. It does not split the epidermis to form bullae.
Autoantibodies to collagen XVII (BP180) cause bullous pemphigoid, with tense subepidermal bullae in older adults.

questions.stem: Her antistreptolysin O titer is within the reference range, while her anti-DNase B titer is markedly increased. Which of the following best explains the normal antistreptolysin O titer?
options: Skin strains of the organism lack the streptolysin O gene
Streptolysin O is poorly immunogenic in young children
Antibody to DNase B neutralizes streptolysin O in serum
Skin lipid cholesterol inactivates streptolysin O
approach: Identify the organism from the culture: S. pyogenes (group A strep), beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive.
Recall that streptolysin O is a cholesterol-binding, oxygen-labile hemolysin.
Apply it: skin lipids bind and inactivate the toxin in impetigo, so little antibody forms. Anti-DNase B is the better marker after skin infection.
questions.why: Streptolysin O is a pore-forming toxin that binds cholesterol in host membranes. In skin infection, cholesterol in skin lipids binds and inactivates it, so the ASO response is weak. Anti-DNase B rises well after both skin and throat infection. Other group A strep factors are M protein (blocks complement and phagocytosis), the hyaluronic acid capsule, streptokinase, and pyrogenic exotoxins. Nephritogenic strains cause glomerulonephritis after either throat or skin infection. Rheumatic fever follows only pharyngitis, which is why it is not expected after impetigo.
whyNot: All group A streptococci make streptolysin O. Skin strains differ in their M protein types, not in this gene.
Children mount a strong ASO response after streptococcal pharyngitis, so the toxin is clearly immunogenic at her age.
Antibodies to DNase B and to streptolysin O target different proteins and do not cross-react.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her facial lesions healed without scarring. In which of the following tissue levels did the bacteria most likely proliferate?
options: Epidermis just below the stratum corneum
Hair follicle extending into the deep dermis
Upper dermis and superficial lymphatics
Subcutaneous tissue and deep fascia
approach: Identify honey-colored crusts in a child as nonbullous impetigo.
Recall that skin infections are named by the depth they reach.
Impetigo stays within the epidermis, which regenerates from the basal layer without a scar.
questions.why: Skin infections follow a sequence: entry through a small break, adherence, colonization, invasion, and spread. The depth reached names the disease. Impetigo stays in the superficial epidermis, under the stratum corneum. Folliculitis involves the hair follicle. Erysipelas involves the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, with a raised, sharp border. Cellulitis reaches the deep dermis and subcutis, an abscess is a walled-off pus collection, and necrotizing fasciitis spreads along the fascia. Because impetigo spares the dermis, it heals without scarring.
whyNot: Correct.
Infection centered on a hair follicle and reaching the deep dermis is a furuncle.
Infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics is erysipelas, which has a raised, sharply demarcated border.
Infection along the deep fascia is necrotizing fasciitis, with pain out of proportion to exam and rapid spread.

questions.stem: Healing of her facial erosions began as the deepest keratinocytes divided to restore the epidermis. Which of the following keratin pairs is characteristic of those dividing cells?
options: Keratins 1 and 10
Keratins 4 and 13
Keratins 5 and 14
Keratins 8 and 18
approach: Identify the layer that renews the epidermis: the stratum basale.
Recall the keratin switch: basal cells make keratins 5 and 14, and cells switch to keratins 1 and 10 as they move into the stratum spinosum.
Match the other pairs to their tissues to exclude them.
questions.why: The stratum basale holds the dividing stem cells of the epidermis, and they express keratins 5 and 14. As cells move up into the stratum spinosum they switch to keratins 1 and 10. In the stratum granulosum they gain keratohyalin granules and lamellar bodies, which release lipids that seal the skin. In the stratum corneum they lose their nuclei and become flat, dead squames. The stratum lucidum appears only in the thick skin of the palms and soles. Mutations in keratins 5 or 14 cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, with blisters through the basal layer.
whyNot: Keratins 1 and 10 are made by suprabasal cells in the stratum spinosum and above, which no longer divide.
Keratins 4 and 13 mark the suprabasal cells of nonkeratinized stratified epithelia such as the oral mucosa and esophagus.
Correct.
Keratins 8 and 18 are found in simple epithelia such as hepatocytes and glandular cells, not in the epidermis.

case: A 24-year-old man comes to the sexual health clinic because of painless bumps on his penis and around his anus for 3 months. He has had three male partners in the past year and uses condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows multiple soft, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like papules 2 to 6 mm in diameter on the penile shaft and perianal skin. A biopsy specimen shows papillomatosis, acanthosis, and hyperkeratosis, with keratinocytes in the upper layers that have wrinkled nuclei surrounded by clear halos. Polymerase chain reaction detects human papillomavirus (HPV) type 6. An HIV test is negative. Diagnosis: anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum).

questions.stem: His roommate received a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. The roommate has dozens of common warts on both hands that keep recurring. Which of the following best explains the roommate's extensive warts?
options: Low IgA levels at mucosal surfaces
Impaired membrane attack complex formation
Reduced neutrophil oxidative burst
Suppressed T cell-mediated immunity
approach: Recall the drugs: tacrolimus blocks calcineurin and IL-2 production, and mycophenolate blocks lymphocyte proliferation.
Recall that clearance of HPV-infected keratinocytes depends on cell-mediated immunity.
Connect them: T cell suppression lets warts spread and persist.
questions.why: Warts are benign HPV-driven proliferations of keratinocytes. Common warts are caused mainly by HPV 2, plantar warts by HPV 1, flat warts by HPV 3 and 10, and anogenital warts by HPV 6 and 11. Histology shows papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and koilocytes, which are keratinocytes with wrinkled nuclei and a clear halo. Most warts regress when T cells recognize infected cells. Patients with weak T cell immunity, such as transplant recipients and people with untreated HIV, develop numerous, persistent warts.
whyNot: IgA deficiency causes recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections such as Giardia. It does not cause widespread warts.
Defects in C5 to C9 predispose to recurrent Neisseria infections.
A defective oxidative burst (chronic granulomatous disease) causes abscesses with catalase-positive bacteria and fungi.
Correct.

questions.stem: He asks whether vaccination would have prevented his warts. The 9-valent HPV vaccine includes types 6 and 11. By which of the following mechanisms does this vaccine mainly protect?
options: Cytotoxic T cells killing E6- and E7-expressing cells
Neutralizing antibody against L1 capsid protein
Replication of attenuated virus in basal keratinocytes
Interferon induction by viral DNA within the particle
approach: Recall what the vaccine contains: recombinant L1 protein that self-assembles into virus-like particles.
These particles carry no viral DNA, so they cannot infect or replicate.
A protein antigen given this way mainly induces neutralizing antibody that blocks infection of basal cells.
questions.why: The HPV vaccine is a subunit vaccine. The L1 major capsid protein is made in yeast and folds into empty shells called virus-like particles. They look like the virus to B cells, so they induce high levels of neutralizing IgG that blocks the virus before it reaches basal keratinocytes. Because there is no viral DNA, there is no E6 or E7 antigen and no replication, so the vaccine prevents new infection but does not treat existing warts. Live attenuated vaccines such as varicella replicate and induce both antibody and cell-mediated immunity.
whyNot: E6 and E7 are not in the vaccine, so it does not induce T cells against infected cells. This is why it does not clear existing infection.
Correct.
Replication of an attenuated virus describes live vaccines such as varicella and MMR. The HPV vaccine contains no live virus.
Virus-like particles contain no viral DNA. Protection comes from antibody, not interferon.

questions.stem: A flat lesion on his anal margin shows high-grade dysplasia, and polymerase chain reaction detects HPV 16. Which of the following best explains how this viral type drives infected cells past the G1 to S checkpoint?
options: E1 protein inducing p21 expression
L1 protein activating TP53 transcription
E7 protein binding and inactivating Rb
E6 protein increasing p53 stability
approach: Recall the G1 to S checkpoint: Rb holds E2F until cyclin D and CDK4/6 phosphorylate it.
Recall the high-risk HPV oncoproteins: E7 binds Rb, and E6 targets p53 for degradation.
Apply it: E7 releases E2F and pushes the cell into S phase.
questions.why: Cell entry into S phase is gated by Rb. Unphosphorylated Rb binds E2F and blocks transcription of S-phase genes. Cyclin D with CDK4/6, then cyclin E with CDK2, phosphorylate Rb and release E2F. p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21, a CDK inhibitor that stops this process, or triggers apoptosis. High-risk HPV types (16, 18) make an E7 protein that binds Rb tightly and frees E2F, and an E6 protein that sends p53 to the proteasome. Low-risk types 6 and 11 make weaker versions, so they cause warts but rarely cancer.
whyNot: E1 is the viral helicase that copies the viral genome. It does not control the host G1 to S checkpoint.
L1 is the capsid protein. It forms the virion shell and has no role in cell cycle control.
Correct.
E6 of high-risk HPV does the opposite. It recruits a ubiquitin ligase that degrades p53.

topics: Rb, E2F, and the G1 to S checkpoint

questions.stem: Morphometric analysis of his penile wart shows an epidermis about three times normal thickness, with more cell layers than normal, keratinocytes of normal size, and orderly maturation toward the surface. Which of the following best describes this change?
options: Hyperplasia from virus-driven keratinocyte division
Hypertrophy from enlargement of individual keratinocytes
Metaplasia from reprogramming of basal stem cells
Dysplasia with loss of orderly maturation
approach: Count, then size: more cell layers with normal-sized cells means more cells.
More cells is hyperplasia, which needs cells that can divide.
Orderly maturation excludes dysplasia, and an unchanged cell type excludes metaplasia.
questions.why: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number. Keratinocytes can divide, so the epidermis responds to growth signals by adding layers. Here the signal is HPV, whose proteins push basal and suprabasal cells to keep dividing. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, typical of cells that cannot divide, such as cardiac and skeletal muscle. A callus is physiologic epidermal hyperplasia from friction. Metaplasia replaces one adult cell type with another, such as squamous metaplasia of the bronchi in smokers. Pathologic hyperplasia and metaplasia can progress to dysplasia, as in the anal lesion driven by HPV 16.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypertrophy would show larger cells, not more layers of normal-sized cells.
Metaplasia changes the type of epithelium. The epidermis here is still keratinizing squamous epithelium.
Dysplasia shows disordered maturation and atypical nuclei, which this lesion lacks.

dx: Pasteurella multocida wound infection after a cat bite
case: A 41-year-old woman comes to urgent care because of pain and swelling of her left hand that began 12 hours after her cat bit her. Her temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows two puncture wounds on the dorsum of the hand with 4 cm of surrounding erythema, warmth, tenderness, and serous drainage. Range of motion of the fingers is full. Culture of the drainage grows small gram-negative coccobacilli that are oxidase positive. Diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida wound infection after a cat bite.

questions.stem: Her brother, who had a splenectomy after a car crash, is bitten on the forearm by his dog. Two days later he develops fever, hypotension, purpura, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
options: Eikenella corrodens
Vibrio vulnificus
Capnocytophaga canimorsus
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae
approach: Identify the exposure: a dog bite.
Identify the host factor: asplenia, which removes the main defense against bloodstream bacteria.
Match both: Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a dog mouth organism, causes fulminant sepsis in asplenic patients.
questions.why: The source of a wound points to the organism. Cat and dog bites carry Pasteurella multocida, which causes fast cellulitis within a day. Capnocytophaga canimorsus, also from dog saliva, causes overwhelming sepsis with purpura and DIC in people without a spleen or with alcohol use disorder. Human bites and clenched-fist injuries carry Eikenella corrodens. Salt water and raw shellfish carry Vibrio vulnificus, fish tanks carry Mycobacterium marinum, and rose thorns carry Sporothrix schenckii.
whyNot: Eikenella corrodens comes from the human mouth and infects human bites and clenched-fist injuries.
Vibrio vulnificus causes bullous cellulitis and sepsis after salt water exposure or raw oysters, especially in liver disease.
Correct.
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae causes a violet cellulitis of the hands in people who handle fish, shellfish, or raw meat.

questions.stem: A clean laceration on her forearm from the same incident was sutured. A biopsy specimen of that laceration taken on day 4 would most likely show which of the following?
options: Macrophages with early granulation tissue
Neutrophils with a fibrin clot only
Myofibroblasts with mature type I collagen
Platelets with no inflammatory cells
approach: Lay out the timeline: hemostasis in minutes, neutrophils in the first 1 to 2 days, macrophages by about day 3.
Granulation tissue (new capillaries and fibroblasts) begins to form around days 3 to 5.
Place day 4 in that timeline.
questions.why: Wound healing proceeds in overlapping phases. Hemostasis forms a platelet and fibrin plug within minutes. Neutrophils arrive within 24 hours, and macrophages replace them by about day 3. Macrophages clear debris and release growth factors such as TGF-beta and VEGF, which start the proliferative phase: granulation tissue with new capillaries, fibroblasts, and type III collagen. Over weeks to months, remodeling replaces type III collagen with type I through zinc-dependent metalloproteinases. A scar regains only about 70 to 80 percent of the strength of normal skin.
whyNot: Correct.
A neutrophil-rich wound with only fibrin describes the first 1 to 2 days.
Mature type I collagen belongs to the remodeling phase, weeks to months later.
A platelet plug without inflammation describes the first minutes after injury.

questions.stem: Her wound heals slowly. She reports eating no fruits or vegetables for several months. Examination shows swollen, bleeding gums and perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs. Which of the following steps of collagen synthesis is most directly impaired?
options: Translation of pro-alpha chains on ribosomes
Hydroxylation of proline residues in the ER
Cleavage of procollagen peptides outside the cell
Lysyl oxidase cross-linking of fibrils outside the cell
approach: Recognize bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and corkscrew hairs as scurvy from vitamin C deficiency.
Recall that prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need vitamin C to keep their iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state.
Without hydroxyproline the triple helix is unstable, so collagen is weak and wounds heal poorly.
questions.why: Collagen synthesis begins with translation of pro-alpha chains rich in glycine, proline, and lysine. In the rough ER, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add hydroxyl groups, which needs vitamin C and Fe2+. Hydroxylysines are then glycosylated, and three chains form a triple helix held by hydrogen bonds from hydroxyproline. Outside the cell, procollagen peptidases cut off the end propeptides, and copper-dependent lysyl oxidase cross-links the fibrils. In scurvy the helix is unstable, so vessels are fragile and wounds lack strong collagen.
whyNot: Translation proceeds normally in scurvy. The defect is a modification made after translation.
Correct.
Failure of procollagen peptidase causes the dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Lysyl oxidase needs copper. Its failure is seen in Menkes disease, with kinky hair and weak vessels.

questions.stem: Two days later an abscess forms at one puncture site. It is incised, drained, and left open to heal from its base. Compared with healing of her sutured laceration, which of the following is most characteristic of healing of this wound?
options: Less granulation tissue and less inflammation
Greater final tensile strength than normal skin
Faster re-epithelialization across a narrow gap
Wound contraction by myofibroblasts
approach: Identify the healing mode: an open wound with separated edges heals by secondary intention.
Recall the features: more inflammation, more granulation tissue, and contraction.
Name the cell that pulls the edges together: the myofibroblast.
questions.why: Healing by primary intention closes a clean incision whose edges are brought together, with little granulation tissue and a thin scar. Healing by secondary intention fills a larger, open defect. It needs more inflammation and granulation tissue, and myofibroblasts, fibroblasts with smooth muscle actin, contract the wound and can shrink it a great deal. Infection, diabetes, ischemia, glucocorticoids, malnutrition, vitamin C or zinc deficiency, and foreign bodies all delay healing, and several apply to this wound.
whyNot: Less granulation tissue and inflammation describe primary intention healing of a sutured wound.
No scar is stronger than normal skin. Scars reach only about 70 to 80 percent of normal strength.
Fast re-epithelialization across a narrow gap describes a sutured incision, not an open wound.
Correct.

case: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician for a skin examination. He has a mole on his upper back that he first noticed as a flat brown spot during adolescence and that has become slightly raised. He reports no itching, bleeding, or recent change. Physical examination shows a 4-mm, round, symmetric, uniformly tan-brown, slightly raised papule with a regular border. It is excised for cosmetic reasons. Microscopic examination shows nests of uniform nevus cells at the dermal-epidermal junction and within the dermis. Cells deeper in the dermis are smaller, contain less pigment, and are arranged in cords. Diagnosis: compound nevocellular nevus.

questions.stem: When this lesion first appeared as a flat brown spot in adolescence, which of the following histologic patterns would it most likely have shown?
options: Nests within the dermis with no junctional component
Nests confined to the dermal-epidermal junction
Single atypical cells scattered through all epidermal layers
Dendritic pigmented cells deep in the reticular dermis
approach: Recall that nevi evolve with age as nests move from the junction into the dermis.
Link shape to location: a flat macule has nests only at the junction, and a raised papule has dermal nests.
So the early, flat lesion was a junctional nevus.
questions.why: Nevocellular nevi begin when a melanocyte acquires an activating BRAF or NRAS mutation, proliferates, and then stops growing through oncogene-induced senescence. Early nevi are junctional: nests sit at the dermal-epidermal junction, and the lesion is flat. Over time nests migrate into the dermis, producing a raised compound nevus with both components. Later the junctional component disappears, leaving an intradermal nevus, often a flesh-colored papule in older adults. Cells that descend deeper become smaller and less pigmented, a benign feature called maturation.
whyNot: A purely dermal nevus is an intradermal nevus. It is the late stage, usually a raised, lightly pigmented papule in older adults.
Correct.
Single atypical cells spreading upward through the epidermis (pagetoid spread) suggest melanoma in situ.
Dendritic pigmented melanocytes deep in the dermis describe a blue nevus, which looks blue-black and does not start as a junctional lesion.

questions.stem: Several other pigmented lesions are present on his skin. Which of the following lesions is most concerning for melanoma?
options: 5-mm round, evenly tan papule, unchanged for 10 years
4-mm dome-shaped, flesh-colored papule that has softened
3-mm symmetric dark brown macule with a regular border
8-mm macule, notched border, black and pink areas
approach: Apply the ABCDE criteria: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter above 6 mm, and evolution.
Check each lesion against them.
Only the 8-mm lesion has an irregular border, several colors, and a large diameter.
questions.why: Benign nevi are usually small (under 6 mm), symmetric, evenly colored, sharply bordered, and stable over time. Melanoma is suggested by asymmetry, irregular or notched borders, multiple colors (black, blue, red, pink, or white areas), diameter above 6 mm, and change in size, shape, or color. Evolution is the most important single sign. Large congenital melanocytic nevi, especially those above 20 cm, carry an increased risk of melanoma.
whyNot: A small, evenly colored lesion that has been stable for years has the features of a benign nevus.
A soft, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papule is typical of an older intradermal nevus that has lost its pigment.
A small, symmetric, evenly dark lesion with a regular border meets no ABCDE criteria.
Correct.

questions.stem: His newborn daughter has a 7-cm blue-gray, flat patch with ill-defined borders over the lumbosacral area. Which of the following best explains this lesion?
options: Melanocytes arrested in the dermis during migration
Proliferating capillary endothelial cells in the dermis
Nests of melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction
Dilated mature capillaries from a GNAQ mutation
approach: Recognize a blue-gray, flat lumbosacral patch in a newborn as dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spot).
Recall that melanocytes come from neural crest and migrate through the dermis to the epidermis.
Cells that stop in the dermis look blue because deep pigment scatters short-wavelength light (the Tyndall effect).
questions.why: Melanocytes arise from the neural crest and migrate through the dermis to reach the basal layer of the epidermis. When some stop in the deep dermis, their melanin appears blue-gray through the overlying skin. This is dermal melanocytosis, most common over the lumbosacral area and in infants with darker skin, and it usually fades in childhood. Congenital melanocytic nevi are brown and often raised, infantile hemangiomas are bright red and grow after birth, and port-wine stains are flat red-purple patches that persist.
whyNot: Correct.
Proliferating endothelial cells form an infantile hemangioma, a bright red lesion that appears in the first weeks and then regresses.
Junctional nests make a brown lesion, as in a congenital or acquired nevus, not a blue-gray one.
A GNAQ mutation causes a port-wine stain, a red to purple patch of dilated capillaries that persists for life.

questions.stem: Molecular testing of his excised nevus shows an activating BRAF V600E mutation, the same mutation found in many melanomas. Which of the following additional changes would most likely be needed for a cell in this nevus to become melanoma?
options: Overexpression of wild-type retinoblastoma protein
Increased expression of p16 (CDKN2A)
Loss of p16 with telomerase reactivation
Loss of VEGF secretion by nevus cells
approach: Recall why nevi stop growing: oncogenic BRAF triggers senescence through p16 and Rb.
Ask what a cell needs to escape: loss of the senescence brake and a way to keep dividing without shortening telomeres.
Pick the change that removes p16 and restores telomerase.
questions.why: Cancer requires several hallmarks: sustained growth signaling (here BRAF), loss of tumor suppressors such as RB and TP53 by two hits, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication through telomerase, angiogenesis driven by VEGF, invasion, a shift to glycolysis (Warburg effect), and immune evasion. In a nevus, BRAF signaling alone induces p16, which keeps Rb active and halts the cell cycle. Melanoma commonly loses CDKN2A (p16) and reactivates telomerase, often through TERT promoter mutations, which lets the BRAF-driven cell keep dividing.
whyNot: More functional Rb would strengthen the G1 arrest that keeps the nevus benign.
p16 is the brake that enforces senescence. More of it would keep the nevus from growing.
Correct.
Tumors need VEGF-driven angiogenesis to grow beyond a small size. Losing VEGF would slow progression.

case: A 21-year-old military recruit is brought to the field medical station after collapsing during a 10-km march in hot, humid weather. He is confused and combative. His rectal temperature is 41.6 °C (106.9 °F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg. His skin is hot and wet with sweat. Laboratory studies show creatine kinase 48,000 U/L (about 25 to 200), potassium 5.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2), and platelet count 62,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). Diagnosis: exertional heat stroke with rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: A second recruit on the same march is dizzy and nauseated, with a rectal temperature of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), heavy sweating, tachycardia, and normal mental status. Which of the following findings best distinguishes the first recruit's condition from that of the second recruit?
options: CNS dysfunction with core temperature over 40 °C (104 °F)
Profuse sweating driven by sympathetic cholinergic fibers
Tachycardia from reduced effective circulating blood volume
Cutaneous vasodilation diverting cardiac output to the skin
approach: Identify the second recruit's picture as heat exhaustion: heat stress with intact mental status.
Recall the definition of heat stroke: core temperature above 40 °C (104 °F) with central nervous system dysfunction.
Find the feature only the first recruit has.
questions.why: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke both come from heat stress. In heat exhaustion, sweating and skin vasodilation are working, and volume depletion causes dizziness, nausea, and tachycardia, but the brain functions normally. Heat stroke is failure of thermoregulation, with core temperature above 40 °C (104 °F) and central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, seizures, or coma. Exertional heat stroke strikes healthy young people during heavy exercise, and they often still sweat. Classic heat stroke strikes older or chronically ill people during heat waves, often with dry skin. Exertional cases often bring rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and DIC, as here.
whyNot: Correct.
Both recruits sweat. Sweating continues in exertional heat stroke, so it does not separate the two.
Both recruits are tachycardic from volume loss and heat. This finding is shared.
Skin vasodilation is the normal heat-loss response in both conditions.

questions.stem: Because of the severe rhabdomyolysis, an inherited muscle disorder is considered. His father once developed masseter rigidity, rising end-tidal CO2, and a temperature of 40.5 °C (104.9 °F) shortly after receiving sevoflurane and succinylcholine. Which of the following best describes the defect in the father's condition?
options: Absent dystrophin anchoring actin to the sarcolemma
Chloride channel loss causing delayed muscle relaxation
Unregulated calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum
Impaired long-chain fatty acid transport into mitochondria
approach: Recognize rigidity, rising CO2, and fever after a volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine as malignant hyperthermia.
Recall the gene: RYR1, the ryanodine receptor calcium release channel of skeletal muscle.
Connect it: uncontrolled calcium release drives sustained contraction, ATP use, CO2 production, and heat.
questions.why: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant disorder, most often from RYR1 mutations. The mutant ryanodine receptor opens too easily when exposed to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, so calcium floods out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Muscles contract continuously, burn ATP, and generate CO2, lactic acid, and heat. Rigidity, hypercarbia, tachycardia, rising temperature, hyperkalemia, and rhabdomyolysis follow. Dantrolene treats it by blocking the ryanodine receptor. Some RYR1 variants are also linked to exertional heat illness and rhabdomyolysis.
whyNot: Absent dystrophin causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy. These boys can have severe reactions to anesthetics, but the mechanism is membrane fragility, not calcium channel failure.
Loss of the muscle chloride channel causes myotonia congenita, with stiffness and slow relaxation after voluntary contraction.
Correct.
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency causes rhabdomyolysis with prolonged exercise or fasting, not a reaction to anesthesia.

questions.stem: He dies of multiorgan failure 3 days later. Electron microscopy of renal tubular cells is performed at autopsy. Which of the following findings indicates irreversible injury?
options: Swelling with dilated endoplasmic reticulum
Blebbing of the plasma membrane
Ribosomes detached from rough endoplasmic reticulum
Amorphous densities within mitochondria
approach: Sort the findings into reversible and irreversible changes.
Reversible changes come from ATP loss: swelling, blebs, ribosome detachment, and fatty change.
Irreversible changes mark mitochondrial and membrane failure: amorphous mitochondrial densities, membrane rupture, and nuclear breakdown.
questions.why: Cell injury starts with ATP depletion, calcium influx, oxidative stress, and membrane damage. Early on, failure of the Na+/K+-ATPase lets water in, so cells swell, the ER dilates, blebs form, and ribosomes detach. These changes reverse if the insult stops. Injury becomes irreversible when mitochondria cannot recover (large amorphous densities from calcium and protein), lysosomal and plasma membranes rupture, and the nucleus shrinks (pyknosis), fragments (karyorrhexis), or fades (karyolysis).
whyNot: Swelling and ER dilation are the first and most common signs of reversible injury.
Plasma membrane blebs form early as the cytoskeleton detaches. They are reversible.
Ribosome detachment reduces protein synthesis and is reversible.
Correct.

questions.stem: In his overheated, poorly perfused skeletal muscle, ATP stores fall. Which of the following changes in the muscle cells most likely results from reduced Na+/K+-ATPase activity?
options: Decreased intracellular sodium with cell shrinkage
Increased intracellular sodium with cell swelling
Increased intracellular potassium with hyperpolarization
Decreased intracellular calcium with relaxation
approach: Recall that the Na+/K+-ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in for each ATP.
When ATP falls, sodium accumulates inside and potassium leaks out.
Water follows the sodium, so cells swell and the membrane depolarizes.
questions.why: The Na+/K+-ATPase keeps intracellular sodium low and potassium high. Because it moves three positive charges out for every two in, it also adds a little directly to the negative resting potential. When ATP is depleted, sodium builds up inside, water follows by osmosis, and the cell swells. This is the earliest change of hypoxic cell injury. Potassium leaks out of the cells, and with muscle breakdown this helps explain his serum potassium of 5.9 mEq/L. The membrane depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes.
whyNot: Pump failure raises intracellular sodium. Cells swell rather than shrink.
Correct.
Potassium leaves the cell when the pump fails, and the membrane depolarizes.
Intracellular calcium rises in ATP depletion because calcium pumps also fail. This activates damaging enzymes.

dx: Partial- and full-thickness thermal burns from a house fire
case: A 45-year-old woman is admitted to the burn unit after being rescued from a house fire. She weighs 70 kg. Her temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. The entire right upper limb is red, moist, and blistered; it blanches with pressure and is very painful to touch. The entire front of the trunk is dry, white, and leathery; it does not blanch and is insensate to pinprick. Her nasal hairs are singed, and she coughs up carbonaceous sputum. Diagnosis: partial-thickness and full-thickness thermal burns with inhalation injury.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the depth of her trunk burn and the total body surface area burned, estimated by the rule of nines?
options: Superficial partial-thickness, 18 percent
Deep partial-thickness, 18 percent
Full-thickness, 18 percent
Full-thickness, 27 percent
approach: Classify depth: dry, white, leathery, insensate skin that does not blanch is full-thickness.
Apply the rule of nines: each upper limb is 9 percent, and the front of the trunk is 18 percent.
Add every partial- and full-thickness area: 9 plus 18 is 27 percent.
questions.why: Burn depth is judged at the bedside. Superficial burns (epidermis only) are red and painful without blisters. Superficial partial-thickness burns reach the papillary dermis and are moist, blistered, blanching, and very painful, like her arm. Deep partial-thickness burns reach the reticular dermis and are less painful and blanch poorly. Full-thickness burns destroy the whole dermis with its nerves and vessels, so they are white or leathery, insensate, and nonblanching. In adults the rule of nines gives 9 percent to the head, 9 percent to each upper limb, 18 percent each to the front and back of the trunk, and 18 percent to each lower limb. Superficial burns are not counted. Large burns cause hypovolemia, a hypermetabolic state, infection with Pseudomonas, and later contracture.
whyNot: Moist, blistered, painful skin is a superficial partial-thickness burn, which describes her arm, not her trunk. The 18 percent also leaves out the arm.
Deep partial-thickness burns still have some sensation and dermal structures. The total also leaves out her arm.
The depth is right, but 18 percent counts only the front of the trunk and leaves out the arm.
Correct.

questions.stem: Ten months later, the grafted areas on her trunk have raised, firm, red scars that remain within the original burn margins and have started to flatten. Which of the following best describes these scars?
options: Hypertrophic scars, likely to regress over time
Keloids, likely to extend beyond the wound
Exuberant granulation tissue blocking re-epithelialization
Wound dehiscence from inadequate collagen
approach: Note the two key features: the scars stay within the wound borders and are flattening.
Recall that hypertrophic scars stay inside the wound and often regress, while keloids grow beyond it and persist.
Choose the option that matches both features.
questions.why: Excess scar tissue takes two forms. Hypertrophic scars are raised but stay within the original wound. They contain mostly type III collagen arranged in bundles parallel to the epidermis and often flatten over months to years. They are very common after burns. Keloids extend beyond the wound edges, contain thick, disorganized type I and III collagen, rarely regress, recur after excision, and favor the earlobes, chest, and shoulders, especially in people with darker skin. Other healing problems are exuberant granulation tissue, dehiscence, and contracture.
whyNot: Correct.
Keloids grow past the wound margins and do not regress. These scars stay within the margins and are flattening.
Exuberant granulation tissue (proud flesh) is soft, red tissue that rises above the skin and blocks epithelial growth during healing, not a firm scar months later.
Dehiscence is reopening of a wound, usually in the first 1 to 2 weeks, from tension, infection, or poor collagen synthesis.

questions.stem: During the first hours she receives large volumes of intravenous fluid. Which of the following fluids, infused alone in large volume, would most likely cause her cells to swell?
options: 0.9% sodium chloride
3% sodium chloride
5% dextrose in water
5% albumin in saline
approach: Separate osmolarity from tonicity: tonicity depends only on solutes that cannot cross cell membranes.
5% dextrose is about isosmotic in the bag, but cells take up and metabolize the glucose.
What remains is free water, which is hypotonic, so water moves into cells and they swell.
questions.why: Water moves by osmosis toward the side with more effective solute. Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles, while tonicity counts only those that stay outside cells and pull water. Normal saline is isotonic, so cell volume does not change. Hypertonic saline draws water out of cells. Dextrose 5% starts at about 250 to 280 mOsm/L, but glucose enters cells and is metabolized, leaving free water that acts as a hypotonic solution. Urea works the same way: it crosses membranes freely, so it is an ineffective osmole that adds osmolarity without tonicity.
whyNot: Normal saline is isotonic. Sodium and chloride stay mostly outside cells, so cell volume does not change.
3% saline is hypertonic. It pulls water out of cells and shrinks them.
Correct.
Albumin in saline is isotonic and stays mostly in the vascular space, where its oncotic pressure holds fluid in vessels.

questions.stem: On day 6 her full-thickness trunk wound develops blue-green exudate with a sweet, grapelike odor. Culture grows oxidase-positive, gram-negative rods. Which of the following best explains why intact skin normally resists colonization by this organism?
options: Keratinocytes secrete IgE into the stratum corneum
Dry, acidic surface with antimicrobial peptides and flora
Moist, neutral surface that favors gram-negative organisms
Melanin absorbs ultraviolet light and kills surface bacteria
approach: Identify the organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative rod that thrives in moist environments.
List the defenses of intact skin: a dry keratinized barrier, acidic pH, sebum fatty acids, shedding of squames, antimicrobial peptides, and competing flora.
A full-thickness burn removes all of these and leaves moist, dead tissue.
questions.why: Healthy skin resists colonization in several ways. The stratum corneum is dry and constantly shed. The surface pH is about 4.5 to 5.5, and fatty acids released from sebum are toxic to many bacteria. Keratinocytes make antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and cathelicidin. Resident flora, including Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes, Corynebacterium, and Malassezia, compete for space and nutrients. Some people also carry S. aureus in the nares. A burn removes this barrier and leaves moist, avascular eschar where Pseudomonas thrives.
whyNot: Keratinocytes do not secrete IgE. IgE is made by plasma cells and binds mast cells. The main secreted antibody at mucosal surfaces is IgA.
Correct.
Intact skin is dry and acidic. A moist, neutral surface is what a burn wound offers and what favors Pseudomonas.
Melanin protects keratinocyte nuclei from UV damage. It does not sterilize the skin surface.

dx: Accidental hypothermia with frostbite of the toes
case: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found lying in the snow on a winter morning. He is drowsy and slurring his speech. His core temperature is 29.5 °C (85.1 °F), pulse is 38/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. He is not shivering. An ECG shows sinus bradycardia, prolonged intervals, and a positive deflection at the junction of the QRS complex and ST segment (Osborn J wave). The toes of both feet are white, hard, and numb. After rewarming, they become swollen with hemorrhagic blisters. Diagnosis: accidental hypothermia with frostbite of the toes.

questions.stem: His brother works on a fishing boat and develops itchy, tender, red-purple papules on several fingers after weeks of cold, damp exposure at temperatures above freezing. Which of the following best explains the brother's lesions?
options: Ice crystals forming in the extracellular fluid
Microvascular thrombosis after tissue freezing
Inflammation from damp cold without freezing
Cryoglobulin immune complexes in small vessels
approach: Note the exposure: damp cold above freezing, repeated over weeks.
Recall that frostbite needs tissue freezing, with ice crystals, endothelial injury, and thrombosis.
Nonfreezing damp cold causes perniosis (chilblains), an inflammatory reaction in small vessels.
questions.why: Frostbite occurs when tissue freezes. Ice crystals form outside cells and draw water out of them, and endothelial injury leads to thrombosis and ischemia when the tissue rewarms, as in this patient's blistered toes. Perniosis (chilblains) follows repeated exposure to damp cold above freezing. Vessels constrict and then react with inflammation, causing itchy or painful red-purple papules on the fingers and toes. In the patient, systemic hypothermia below 35 °C (95 °F) slows the heart, produces Osborn J waves, and raises the risk of arrhythmias. Shivering usually stops once core temperature falls below about 32 °C (89.6 °F).
whyNot: Ice crystal formation requires tissue freezing, which did not occur in the brother.
Thrombosis after freezing and rewarming is the mechanism of frostbite, as in the patient's toes.
Correct.
Cryoglobulinemia causes purpura and vasculitis from immune complexes that precipitate in the cold, often with hepatitis C. It is a systemic disease that does not depend on damp exposure.

questions.stem: Unlike this patient, a healthy newborn exposed to cold produces heat mainly without shivering. Which of the following is the main source of that heat?
options: Thyroid hormone induction of Na+/K+-ATPase
Uncoupling protein 1 in brown adipose tissue
Myosin ATP hydrolysis in skeletal muscle
Cutaneous vasoconstriction reducing heat loss
approach: Note the age: newborns shiver poorly.
Recall nonshivering thermogenesis: sympathetic stimulation of brown fat through beta-3 receptors.
Name the protein: UCP1 (thermogenin) lets protons leak back into the matrix, releasing energy as heat.
questions.why: The body keeps heat by cutaneous vasoconstriction and piloerection, and makes heat by shivering, thyroid hormone, and nonshivering thermogenesis. Brown fat cells are packed with mitochondria. Norepinephrine acting on beta-3 receptors activates UCP1 (thermogenin), which lets protons flow back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without making ATP, so the energy is released as heat. Newborns have a large share of brown fat around the neck, between the shoulders, and near the kidneys, and they shiver poorly, so they rely on it. Thyroid hormone raises heat production too, but over days, not minutes.
whyNot: Thyroid hormone increases Na+/K+-ATPase and metabolic rate, but this takes days and is not the newborn's main immediate source of heat.
Correct.
Myosin ATP hydrolysis during shivering is the main source of extra heat in cold adults, but newborns shiver poorly.
Vasoconstriction conserves heat. It does not produce heat.

questions.stem: Rewarming restores blood flow to his toes, and reperfusion generates reactive oxygen species. Glutathione peroxidase in the reperfused cells converts hydrogen peroxide to water. Which of the following combinations is required to keep this enzyme working?
options: Copper and zinc with NADH from glycolysis
Manganese with NADH from the mitochondrial citric acid cycle
Heme iron with FADH2 from mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation
Selenium with NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway
approach: Recall the cofactor of glutathione peroxidase: selenium.
Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione and turns it into oxidized glutathione.
Glutathione reductase regenerates it using NADPH, which comes from G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway.
questions.why: Cells detoxify reactive oxygen species with a chain of enzymes. Superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn in the cytosol, Mn in mitochondria) turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide. Catalase and glutathione peroxidase turn hydrogen peroxide into water. Glutathione peroxidase contains selenium and uses reduced glutathione, which glutathione reductase must regenerate with NADPH. That NADPH comes from glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the pentose phosphate pathway. This is why G6PD deficiency leaves red cells exposed to oxidant damage.
whyNot: Copper and zinc are cofactors of cytosolic superoxide dismutase, not glutathione peroxidase, and NADH does not regenerate glutathione.
Manganese is the cofactor of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase. NADH from the citric acid cycle feeds the electron transport chain.
Heme iron is the cofactor of catalase, which does not need a reducing agent. FADH2 feeds the electron transport chain.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over the next 3 weeks, two toes become black, dry, shriveled, and sharply demarcated from viable tissue. Microscopic examination of an amputated toe would most likely show which of the following patterns?
options: Coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines
Liquefactive necrosis from neutrophil enzyme digestion
Caseous necrosis surrounded by granulomas
Fibrinoid necrosis of small arterial walls
approach: Recognize black, dry, shriveled, demarcated toes as dry gangrene.
Recall that dry gangrene is ischemic coagulative necrosis of a limb.
Coagulative necrosis keeps the ghost outlines of cells because proteins denature before enzymes digest them.
questions.why: Necrosis types match their settings. Coagulative necrosis follows ischemia in most solid organs, such as a myocardial infarct, and preserves tissue architecture with ghost cells. Gangrenous necrosis is ischemic necrosis of a limb. Dry gangrene is mainly coagulative, while wet gangrene adds bacterial infection and liquefaction. Liquefactive necrosis occurs in brain infarcts and abscesses, caseous necrosis in tuberculosis and some fungal infections, fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis and breast trauma, and fibrinoid necrosis in vasculitis and malignant hypertension.
whyNot: Correct.
Liquefactive necrosis follows bacterial infection or brain infarction. It would fit wet gangrene, with swelling and pus.
Caseous necrosis with granulomas is typical of tuberculosis.
Fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls is seen in vasculitis and malignant hypertension.

case: A 36-year-old utility line worker is brought to the trauma center after his right hand touched a 7,200-volt power line. He briefly lost consciousness. His temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. There is a 1-cm charred wound on the right palm and a 1-cm exit wound on the left heel. The right forearm is tense, swollen, and painful with passive finger extension. Serum creatine kinase is 32,000 U/L (about 25 to 200), and potassium is 7.0 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). Urine is dark brown, and dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. Diagnosis: high-voltage electrical injury with rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his skin wounds are small while his forearm muscle damage is extensive?
options: Deep tissues of low resistance carry most of the current
Skin offers lower resistance than muscle to current flow
Current spreads mainly along the skin surface
Muscle is injured mainly by the flash of an electrical arc
approach: Recall that dry skin has high resistance and nerves, vessels, and muscle have low resistance.
Once current crosses the skin at the contact point, it travels through the deep, low-resistance tissues.
Heat produced along that path destroys muscle and nerve under nearly intact skin.
questions.why: Electrical injury is like an iceberg: small entry and exit wounds hide extensive deep damage. Current crosses the skin at the contact points and then follows the low-resistance tissues, such as nerves, vessels, and muscle, generating heat and breaking cell membranes along the way. Bone has high resistance and heats up, which adds to injury of the muscle beside it. Muscle necrosis causes compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and myoglobinuric kidney injury. Current crossing the heart can cause arrhythmias. Lightning causes cardiac arrest and fern-like Lichtenberg figures on the skin.
whyNot: Correct.
Dry skin has a higher resistance than muscle, which is why the skin wounds stay small once current enters the deep tissues.
Current that stays on the surface would cause wide skin burns, not deep muscle necrosis.
An arc flash causes surface thermal burns. It does not explain deep muscle necrosis under intact skin.

questions.stem: Over the next hour he develops generalized muscle weakness and decreased deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following best explains the reduced excitability of his nerves and muscles?
options: Hyperpolarization moving the membrane away from threshold
Opening of more voltage-gated sodium channels at rest
Increased potassium efflux through leak channels
Sustained depolarization inactivating sodium channels
approach: Note his serum potassium of 7.0 mEq/L.
High extracellular potassium shrinks the potassium gradient, so the resting membrane potential depolarizes.
A sustained depolarization closes the inactivation gates of voltage-gated sodium channels, so fewer channels can open and cells fire poorly.
questions.why: The resting potential depends mainly on the potassium gradient. Hyperkalemia raises extracellular potassium, makes the potassium equilibrium potential less negative, and depolarizes cells. A small depolarization first raises excitability, but sustained depolarization closes the inactivation gates of voltage-gated sodium channels. With fewer sodium channels available, action potentials weaken or fail, causing weakness, reduced reflexes, and dangerous cardiac conduction changes. Hypokalemia does the opposite: it hyperpolarizes the membrane and moves it away from threshold.
whyNot: Hyperpolarization is the effect of hypokalemia, which also causes weakness, but by moving the membrane farther from threshold.
Sustained depolarization reduces the number of sodium channels available to open.
Potassium efflux falls when extracellular potassium is high, because the outward gradient is smaller.
Correct.

questions.stem: On day 3 the necrotic forearm muscle becomes swollen with crepitus, bronze skin discoloration, and thin, foul-smelling brown drainage. Gram stain shows large gram-positive rods and few neutrophils. Which of the following toxin activities most directly causes the tissue destruction?
options: Blocking glycine release from spinal interneurons
Phospholipase hydrolysis of cell membrane lecithin
Cleavage of SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2
approach: Recognize crepitus, bronze skin, foul drainage, and large gram-positive rods in dead muscle as gas gangrene from Clostridium perfringens.
Recall its main toxin: alpha toxin, a lecithinase (phospholipase C).
Lecithinase breaks cell membranes, causing myonecrosis and hemolysis and killing neutrophils, which explains why so few are seen.
questions.why: Clostridium perfringens is an anaerobic, gram-positive rod that grows in dead, poorly perfused muscle. Its alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that splits lecithin in cell membranes, destroying muscle cells, red cells, and leukocytes. Gas from fermentation produces crepitus. Few neutrophils are seen because the toxin destroys them. Clostridium tetani in a puncture wound makes tetanospasmin, which travels to the spinal cord and blocks release of GABA and glycine from inhibitory interneurons, causing spastic paralysis.
whyNot: Blocking glycine and GABA release from inhibitory interneurons is the action of tetanospasmin, which causes spastic paralysis without tissue necrosis.
Correct.
Cleaving SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction is the action of botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid paralysis.
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 is the action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.

questions.stem: Assume an intracellular potassium concentration of 140 mEq/L in his skeletal muscle. At body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F), the value of 2.303RT/F is about 61 mV. Which of the following is closest to the potassium equilibrium potential of his muscle cells at his current serum potassium?
options: -94 mV
-79 mV
-61 mV
approach: Write the Nernst equation for a cation: E = 61 mV x log10 ([K+] outside / [K+] inside).
Plug in his values: 7.0 / 140 = 0.05, and log10 of 0.05 is about -1.3.
Multiply: 61 x -1.3 is about -79 mV, less negative than the normal value of about -94 mV.
questions.why: The Nernst equation gives the membrane potential at which an ion's chemical and electrical gradients balance. For potassium at body temperature, E = 61 mV x log10 ([K+]o / [K+]i). With normal serum potassium of 4 mEq/L, the ratio is 4/140, and E is about -94 mV. At 7.0 mEq/L the ratio is 1/20, and E is about -79 mV. At rest, potassium leak channels make the membrane most permeable to potassium, so the resting potential sits near this value, as the Goldman equation predicts. Impermeant intracellular anions (the Gibbs-Donnan effect) help hold potassium inside the cell. A rise in serum potassium therefore depolarizes his cells.
whyNot: About -106 mV would need a lower serum potassium than normal, as in hypokalemia.
About -94 mV is the normal value with serum potassium of 4 mEq/L, not his current value.
Correct.
About -61 mV would need a tenfold ratio, a serum potassium of 14 mEq/L.
